## Climatological Context and Study Area Description

Birjand, the capital of South Khorasan Province in eastern Iran, features a semi-arid to arid climate characterized by sharp daily and seasonal temperature fluctuations. In this study, I analyzed the trends of key temperature parameters and the Heat Index for Birjand over a 13-year period (2013–2025) using daily meteorological records. The objective of this report is to deliver a structured, data-driven statistical analysis suitable for evaluating localized climate dynamics and environmental risks.

## Long-Term Temperature Trend Analysis (2013–2025)

To extract long-term temperature signals from seasonal noise, I applied non-parametric LOESS (Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing) to the daily mean temperature time series. The smoothed curve reveals long-term thermal variability across the study period, with the smoothed baseline temperature starting at approximately 12.0 °C in 2013, fluctuating between 13.0 °C and 14.3 °C from 2014 through 2023 (with a slight dip near 12.8 °C in 2019–2020), and rising steadily from 2024 toward approximately 17.0 °C to 17.5 °C by late 2025. Concurrently, daily mean temperatures span from typical winter troughs of approximately −5.0 °C to −9.0 °C (with a severe historical cold drop plunging to nearly −14.0 °C in early 2023) to summer peaks of approximately 28.0 °C to 30.0 °C (reaching 31.0 °C to 32.0 °C during peak warm events).

![](../result/birjand/long-term%20temperature%20overview%20(2013–2025).png)

## Seasonal Dynamics and Ramadan Temperature Anomalies

The 2024 daily mean temperature time series clearly demonstrates the expected sinusoidal seasonal cycle
. To evaluate temperature anomalies during specific temporal windows, I calculated the 30-day rolling average temperature on the final day of Ramadan and compared it against historical data for the same calendar date across all study years
. For 2025, with Ramadan spanning from February 28 to March 29, the 30-day rolling average on the final day (March 29, 2025) was recorded at 8.16 °C, which is lower than the historical mean of 8.59 °C for that calendar date
.

![](../result/birjand/yearly%20temperature%20(2024).png)

![](../result/birjand/30-day%20Rolling%20Avg%20on%20Last%20Day%20of%20Ramadan%202025%20vs%20Past%20Years.png)

## Monthly Heat Index Trends and Statistical Testing

By fitting Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression models and executing the non-parametric Mann-Kendall test on monthly mean Heat Index values, I evaluated temperature trends for each month across the 13-year period. Statistically significant warming trends were identified in only two of the twelve months:
**July**: Regression slope of +0.15 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +1.81 °C, p ≈ 0.008–0.024).
**November**: Regression slope of +0.30 °C/year (cumulative change ≈ +3.54 °C, p ≈ 0.010–0.024).
In the remaining ten months, no statistically significant upward or downward trends were detected (p > 0.05). The July Heat Index increase may impact urban water demand and cooling energy consumption, whereas the marked warming in November alters heating demand, agricultural water requirements, and localized frost risk patterns.

**Statistical Terminology & Methodological Note:**

**$p$-value ($\text{lm\_p}$ / $\text{mk\_p}$)**: A measure of statistical significance representing the probability that an observed trend occurred due to random variability. A threshold of $p < 0.05$ denotes a statistically significant trend at the 95% confidence level.

**Mann-Kendall Test (MK / $\text{mk\_p}$)**: A non-parametric rank correlation test used in climatology to confirm whether a monotonic upward or downward trend exists without assuming a normal data distribution.

**Kendall’s Tau ($\tau$ / $\text{mk\_tau}$)**: A non-parametric correlation coefficient ranging from $-1$ to $+1$ that measures the strength and direction of a monotonic trend (positive values indicate an upward trajectory).

**Classification Criteria**: A monthly warming trend is classified as statistically significant only when both the OLS regression ($\text{lm\_p} < 0.05$) and the Mann-Kendall test ($\text{mk\_p} < 0.05$) indicate significant upward shifts.

**Note on Monthly Heat Index Plots**: Blue points represent years with a mean Heat Index at or below the overall multi-year average, while red points represent years above the overall average.

## Extreme Temperature Event Assessment

I defined extreme temperature days as those exceeding two standard deviations (±2 SD) from the 30-day rolling mean. Based on this threshold:
August recorded the highest frequency of extreme days, totaling 54 days (46 very cold and 8 very hot).
October (43 days, predominantly very cold) and November (40 days, all very cold) followed in frequency.
Very hot days occurred most frequently in June (23 days) and March (22 days).
February displayed substantial thermal instability, recording 20 extreme days out of ~28–29 days (~69–71% of the month), evenly split between 10 very hot and 10 very cold days. Coinciding with the Persian month of Bahman, this extreme intra-month thermal variability intensifies bioclimatic stress and potential respiratory health risks in Birjand.

![](../result/birjand/extreme%20temperature%20days%20by%20month%20(hot%20vs%20cold).png)

## Annual Share of Ramadan Extremes vs. Full Year

I evaluated the proportion of annual extreme temperature days occurring specifically within Ramadan relative to full-year totals. For instance, in 2018, 4 of the 32 total annual extreme temperature days coincided with the month of Ramadan.

![](../result/birjand/year-by-year%20comparison%20-%20Extreme%20days%20in%20Ramadan%20vs.%20full%20year.png)
